steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the overview section of an encyclopedia article on arithmetic circuit complexity: what upper and lower bounding the complexity of a polynomial means, how it differs from Boolean circuit complexity, and the main known upper and lower bounds.

steps.name: skeleton_outline

- Formal polynomials, not functions; contrast with Boolean circuits
- Upper bounds: matrix product, determinant, permanent
- Lower bounds: what is known, the main open problem
- Restricted models of computation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Given a polynomial f, we can ask what the best way to compute it is, for example what the smallest size of a circuit computing f is. There are two parts to the answer. The first part is finding some circuit that computes f, and this is usually called upper bounding the complexity of f. The second part is showing that no other circuit can do better, and this is called lower bounding the complexity of f. These two tasks are strongly related, but proving lower bounds is usually harder, because to prove a lower bound you need to argue about all circuits at the same time.

We are interested here in the formal computation of polynomials and not in the functions that the polynomials define. For example, take the polynomial x^2 +x; over the field of two elements it represents the zero function, but it is not the zero polynomial. This is one difference between studying arithmetic circuits and studying Boolean circuits. In Boolean complexity people are mostly interested in computing a function and not some representation of it (here, a representation by a polynomial). This is one of the reasons why Boolean complexity is harder than arithmetic complexity. Studying arithmetic circuits can also be seen as one of the intermediate steps towards studying the Boolean case, which we hardly understand.

### Upper bounds

Some clever circuits (or algorithms) were found as part of studying the complexity of computing polynomials. A well-known example is Strassen's algorithm for matrix product. Computing the product of two n \times n matrices the straightforward way needs a circuit of size order n^3. Strassen showed that in fact we can multiply two matrices with a circuit of size roughly n^{2.807}. The basic idea of Strassen is a clever way of multiplying 2 \times 2 matrices. This idea is the starting point for the best theoretical way of multiplying two matrices, which takes time roughly n^{2.376}.

- determinant: naive roughly n!; polynomial-size circuits known, but depth linear in n
  - Berkowitz: size polynomial in n, depth O(\log^2(n))
- permanent: naive roughly n!; best known roughly 2^n via Ryser's formula (depth three circuit)

### Lower bounds

- knowledge very limited; degree 2^{2^n} needs size roughly 2^n, so main goal is small degree (polynomial in n)
- counting arguments: hard polynomials of polynomial degree exist, but don't help understanding
- main open problem: explicit polynomial of polynomial degree requiring superpolynomial circuits
- state of the art \Omega(n \log d) for x_1^d + \cdots + x_n^d (Strassen; Baur and Strassen)
  - Strassen via Bézout's theorem; Baur and Strassen partial derivatives in O(s)
  - example of upper bound helping a lower bound
- restricted models: monotone, constant depth, multilinear; studied extensively

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Given a polynomial f, we can ask what the best way to compute it is, for example what the smallest size of a circuit computing f is. There are two parts to the answer. The first part is finding some circuit that computes f, and this is usually called upper bounding the complexity of f. The second part is showing that no other circuit can do better, and this is called lower bounding the complexity of f. These two tasks are strongly related, but proving lower bounds is usually harder, because to prove a lower bound you need to argue about all circuits at the same time.

We are interested here in the formal computation of polynomials and not in the functions that the polynomials define. For example, take the polynomial x^2 +x; over the field of two elements it represents the zero function, but it is not the zero polynomial. This is one difference between studying arithmetic circuits and studying Boolean circuits. In Boolean complexity people are mostly interested in computing a function and not some representation of it (here, a representation by a polynomial). This is one of the reasons why Boolean complexity is harder than arithmetic complexity. Studying arithmetic circuits can also be seen as one of the intermediate steps towards studying the Boolean case, which we hardly understand.

### Upper bounds

Some clever circuits (or algorithms) were found as part of studying the complexity of computing polynomials. A well-known example is Strassen's algorithm for matrix product. Computing the product of two n \times n matrices the straightforward way needs a circuit of size order n^3. Strassen showed that in fact we can multiply two matrices with a circuit of size roughly n^{2.807}. The basic idea of Strassen is a clever way of multiplying 2 \times 2 matrices. This idea is the starting point for the best theoretical way of multiplying two matrices, which takes time roughly n^{2.376}.

The determinant of an n \times n matrix is another interesting story. Computing the determinant the naive way needs circuits of size roughly n!. But we know that there are circuits of size polynomial in n for computing the determinant. These circuits have depth that is linear in n, though. Berkowitz improved this: he gave a circuit of size polynomial in n, but of depth O(\log^2(n)).

The best known circuit for the permanent of an n \times n matrix is also worth mentioning. Like for the determinant, the naive circuit for the permanent has size roughly n!. But for the permanent the best known circuit has size roughly 2^n, and it is given by Ryser's formula: for an n \times n matrix X = (x_{i,j}),

\operatorname{perm}(X)=(-1)^n\sum_{S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}}(-1)^ \prod_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in S} x_{i,j}

(this is a depth three circuit).

### Lower bounds

Our knowledge about proving lower bounds is very limited. Because we study the computation of formal polynomials, we know that polynomials of very large degree need large circuits, for example a polynomial of degree 2^{2^n} needs a circuit of size roughly 2^n. So the main goal is proving lower bounds for polynomials of small degree, say polynomial in n. Actually, counting arguments tell us, as in many areas of mathematics, that there are polynomials of polynomial degree that need circuits of superpolynomial size. But these counting arguments usually don't improve our understanding of computation. The main open problem in this area of research is the following: find an explicit polynomial of polynomial degree that requires circuits of superpolynomial size.

The best known result is a \Omega(n \log d) lower bound for the size of a circuit computing for example the polynomial x_1^d + \cdots + x_n^d, given by Strassen and by Baur and Strassen. In more detail, Strassen used Bézout's theorem to show that any circuit that computes the n polynomials x_1^d, \ldots, x_n^d simultaneously has size \Omega(n \log d). Later Baur and Strassen showed that if you are given an arithmetic circuit of size s that computes a polynomial f, you can construct a new circuit of size at most O(s) that computes f and also all the n partial derivatives of f. The partial derivatives of x_1^d + \cdots + x_n^d are dx_1^{d-1}, \ldots, dx_n^{d-1}, so the lower bound of Strassen applies to x_1^d + \cdots + x_n^d too. This is an example where an upper bound helps to prove lower bounds, since the circuit construction of Baur and Strassen implies a lower bound for more general polynomials.

Because we are not able to prove lower bounds, we look at simpler models of computation. Some examples are monotone circuits (where all the field elements are nonnegative real numbers), constant depth circuits, and multilinear circuits (where every gate computes a multilinear polynomial). These restricted models have been studied a lot and some understanding and results were obtained.
